newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Barbra Streisand admits she loves to be in control.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Barbra Streisand admits she loves to be in control.

text.p: When it comes to filmmaking, Barbra Streisand admits she is a control freak -- and proud of it.
"I used to be embarrassed and defensive about it," the legendary singer, actress and director said while promoting her new film, "The Mirror Has Two Faces."

"Control, what do you mean, control?" she said, recalling her initial reaction to scathing reports about skirmishes and script problems on sets of her earlier movies. "But now I say: 'What, are you kidding? Of course I want utter and complete control over every product I do.' The audience buys my work because I do control it, because I am a perfectionist, because I care deeply," she told a recent news conference.

Streisand directed "Mirror" and also stars in it as a college professor named Rose who enters a platonic marriage with a math professor (Jeff Bridges) who is a self-described "sexaholic." The making of the romantic comedy, which opens in the United States on Friday, was marked by the reports of dissension and staff turnover that usually swirl around a Streisand film.
Nevertheless, Streisand's co-stars, including Bridges, Lauren Bacall and Mimi Rogers, praised her filmmaking abilities.

Born in Brooklyn on April 24, 1942, Streisand has become one of the best known entertainers. She won an Oscar in 1968 for her debut movie performance as Fanny Brice in "Funny Girl" and also won five Emmy Awards for her television special "My Name is Barbra" and many Grammy Awards for her recordings.

Many fans hope she will take home the Oscar for directing after failing to receive nominations for her earlier directing efforts, which include "Yentl" and "The Prince of Tides." "Yentl" won an Academy Award for its score and was nominated for four others, but Oscar voters snubbed Streisand and failed to nominate her in a single category.

While she declined to comment about the Oscars, she said she turned to directing to have more control over her work. "As an actress I would sometimes think: Why is that director letting that actor get away with that level of performance? He can get much more out of that actor. So I decided to take more control over my work and I became a director."

While members of the film's cast say Streisand is indeed a perfectionist with an iron will, they also say she is a great collaborator, listener and nurturer. "I found it incredible working with her. She's remarkably intelligent. I learned a great deal from watching her," said Rogers, who plays Streisand's prettier sister in "Mirror."

"What truly defines what she's about as an artist is specificity. Part of the reason why she gets this reputation for being so demanding is this attention for detail that takes something out of the realm from ordinary into the extraordinary," Rogers told Reuters.
"What I observed in watching her is that she'll get a clear picture in her head of how she wants things to be and she's constitutionally incapable of settling for anything less than that."

Streisand says a not-so-happy childhood and being raised by a single parent inspired her at a young age to want to be a star. "I was a strange kid, an outcast. As a teenager, I was kind of lonely and had only one date in high school. I wanted to be an actress, to escape real life and go into this world of the imagination, of make believe," she said.
"That's probably when I decided to create life, make it happen the way I wanted it to be."

While Streisand has indeed created a fantastic life for herself at the price of sometimes being viewed as an egomaniac, she feels this perception comes from people who are intimidated by a woman in power. "I think it's a sexist attitude, definitely. It still hurts, after all these years. I'm always kind of shocked by it, but that's the way it has to be until it changes."
